title: What is `pathGlobFilter` — a Spark read option to filter files by glob pattern when reading from a directory (e.g., `option("pathGlobFilter", "*.csv")`) — and how does it differ from partition discovery?

s1_definition.profdef: `pathGlobFilter` is a Spark DataFrameReader option that restricts which files inside a directory are read, based on a glob pattern matched against the file name. It filters files by name only, without affecting how directories are traversed or how partition columns are inferred. It is different from partition discovery, which is Spark's automatic mechanism that reads the directory structure of a partitioned dataset, turns folder names like `year=2026/month=10` into columns, and uses them for partition pruning.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India keeps a storage room full of mixed documents: trade files ending in dot csv, scanned images ending in dot jpg, and temporary files ending in dot tmp. When you ask a clerk to bring you "the trade data from this room", `pathGlobFilter` is the instruction "only pick up files whose name ends in dot csv, ignore the images and temp files". It is purely a name filter on individual files. Partition discovery is a completely different idea: it is the clerk reading the labeled shelf structure, like "Year 2026 shelf, October drawer", and automatically tagging each file with which shelf and drawer it came from, so you can later say "only the October drawer" and skip the rest.
s1_definition.oneliner: `pathGlobFilter` keeps only files whose names match a glob pattern, while partition discovery turns folder-name structure into columns for pruning; one filters files, the other derives partition metadata.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `pathGlobFilter` is a Spark DataFrameReader option that restricts which files inside a directory are read, based on a glob pattern matched against the file name. It filters files by name only, without affecting how directories are traversed or how partition columns are inferred. It is different from partition discovery, which is Spark's automatic mechanism that reads the directory structure of a partitioned dataset, turns folder names like `year=2026/month=10` into columns, and uses them for partition pruning.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India keeps a storage room full of mixed documents: trade files ending in dot csv, scanned images ending in dot jpg, and temporary files ending in dot tmp. When you ask a clerk to bring you "the trade data from this room", `pathGlobFilter` is the instruction "only pick up files whose name ends in dot csv, ignore the images and temp files". It is purely a name filter on individual files. Partition discovery is a completely different idea: it is the clerk reading the labeled shelf structure, like "Year 2026 shelf, October drawer", and automatically tagging each file with which shelf and drawer it came from, so you can later say "only the October drawer" and skip the rest.

**One line to remember:** `pathGlobFilter` keeps only files whose names match a glob pattern, while partition discovery turns folder-name structure into columns for pruning; one filters files, the other derives partition metadata.

sections.s2_technical:
When you point Spark at a directory with `spark.read.csv("/lake/landing")`, by default it tries to read every file under that path. Often a landing directory contains a mix of files you want and files you do not, such as the actual data files alongside manifest files, success markers, log files, or files from another format. The `pathGlobFilter` option lets you restrict to just the files you want by matching a glob against the file name, for example `.option("pathGlobFilter", "*.csv")` reads only files ending in csv, or `.option("pathGlobFilter", "trades_*.parquet")` reads only the parquet files whose name starts with trades underscore. The pattern is matched against the file name component, not the full path, and it supports standard glob wildcards like star for any characters and question mark for a single character.

This is purely a file-name filter and it does nothing about directory structure or partition columns. Partition discovery is the separate, automatic feature where Spark recognizes a Hive-style directory layout such as `/lake/trades/trade_date=2026-10-30/part-0000.parquet`, extracts `trade_date` as a column with the value from the folder name, and records it so the planner can prune partitions when you filter on it. Partition discovery is controlled by things like `basePath` and the `spark.sql.sources.partitionColumnTypeInference` settings, and it happens regardless of `pathGlobFilter`. You can use both together: `pathGlobFilter` narrows which files within the discovered partitions are read, while partition discovery still turns the folder names into columns.

There are related but distinct options worth separating in your mind. `recursiveFileLookup` set to true tells Spark to recurse into subdirectories but disables partition discovery, treating everything as a flat set of files, which is useful when folders are organizational rather than partition columns. `modifiedBefore` and `modifiedAfter` filter files by their modification timestamp rather than name. `pathGlobFilter` is specifically the name-pattern filter. A senior-level nuance is that `pathGlobFilter` filters during file listing, so it reduces the number of files opened and read, but it does not give you partition pruning on data values; if you want to skip whole date ranges efficiently you rely on partition discovery plus a filter on the partition column, not on a glob. Another nuance is that in object stores, listing is expensive, and combining `pathGlobFilter` with a well-chosen base path avoids listing irrelevant files, which both speeds up the job and reduces cost. The practical rule is to use `pathGlobFilter` to exclude non-data files like markers and logs, and to rely on partition discovery with predicate filters for pruning by data values like dates.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, an upstream system drops files into a landing directory that is partitioned by trade date, but each date folder contains not only the trade CSV files but also a manifest file, a dot success marker, and occasional dot tmp files from interrupted uploads. The first version of the reader pointed at the directory and failed, because Spark tried to parse the manifest and marker files as CSV and hit malformed-record errors. This is exactly the problem pathGlobFilter solves: you only want the files whose names match the data pattern, and you want Spark to ignore the rest.

This is exactly how pathGlobFilter works. Setting the option to the trade file pattern makes Spark list and read only the matching CSV files and skip the manifest, marker, and temp files entirely.

Problem 2 — The team also wanted to keep the automatic trade date column that comes from the folder names so they could prune by date, and they worried that adding the glob filter would break that. It does not: partition discovery still reads the folder structure and derives the trade date column, while pathGlobFilter independently filters files by name. The two features operate on different things, so they compose cleanly.

Because a real Spark reader is heavy, this runnable demo simulates a partitioned landing directory on the local file system and a tiny reader that applies both features. We create date folders containing data CSVs plus non-data files. A `GlobMatcher` compiles a glob to a matcher. A `PartitionDiscoverer` extracts the trade date column from folder names. A `LandingReader` lists files, applies the glob filter, derives partition columns, and reports which files it read and skipped and what partition value each got. The demo proves the non-data files are skipped and the trade date column is still derived.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
landing:
  base-path: /tmp/nbi-landing/trades
  path-glob-filter: "trades_*.csv"     # only data files
  partition-column: trade_date         # from folder names trade_date=...
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a landing directory with two date folders. The folder for the twenty-ninth holds two trade CSVs plus a success marker and a manifest, and the folder for the thirtieth holds two trade CSVs plus a temp upload file.

Step 1: The reader walks the whole directory tree and collects every regular file, which includes the trade CSVs, the success marker, the manifest, and the temp file.

Step 2: For each file the glob matcher checks the file name against the pattern trades underscore star dot csv. The trade CSVs match, so they pass. The success marker, the manifest, and the temp file do not match, so they are skipped and logged as skipped by the path glob filter.

Step 3: For each file that passes the glob, the partition discoverer looks at the parent folder name, sees the trade date prefix, and extracts the date value. The trade files in the twenty-ninth folder get the twenty-ninth as their trade date, and those in the thirtieth folder get the thirtieth.

Step 4: The reader records each read file along with its derived trade date column value, proving that the glob filter excluded the non-data files while partition discovery still produced the trade date column from the folder names.

Step 5: The final log lists exactly the four trade CSV files that became DataFrame input, each tagged with its correct trade date, and reports that three non-data files were skipped.

sections.s6_takeaway:
pathGlobFilter is a Spark read option that restricts which files inside a directory get read, by matching a glob pattern against the file name. You set it like a reader option with a pattern such as star dot csv or trades underscore star dot parquet, and Spark only lists and reads the files whose names match, ignoring everything else. It is purely a file-name filter and it is applied during file listing, so it reduces the number of files opened, which both speeds up the job and, on object stores where listing costs money, reduces cost.

The key distinction the question is getting at is that pathGlobFilter is not partition discovery. Partition discovery is a separate, automatic feature where Spark recognizes a Hive-style folder layout like trade date equals a value, extracts that folder name as a column, and uses it for partition pruning when you filter on it. pathGlobFilter never touches directory structure or partition columns, it only decides which individual files to read, so the two features operate on different things and compose cleanly: the glob narrows which files within the discovered partitions are read, while partition discovery still derives the partition column from the folder names. I also keep the related options straight, because recursive file lookup recurses into subfolders but disables partition discovery, and modified before and modified after filter by timestamp rather than name.

At the National Bank of India this solved a real ingestion failure. Our landing zone was partitioned by trade date, but each date folder contained not just the trade CSVs but also a success marker, a manifest, and occasional temp files from interrupted uploads, and the reader kept failing because Spark tried to parse those non-data files as CSV. Setting pathGlobFilter to the trade file pattern made Spark read only the data files and skip the markers, manifests, and temp files, and the trade date column was still derived from the folder names because partition discovery is independent of the glob. The rule I follow is to use pathGlobFilter to exclude non-data files and rely on partition discovery with a predicate on the partition column when I actually want to prune by data values like a date range.
